description: Sugar, tea and coffee — how empire transformed daily life, public debate and the politics of slavery.
content_html:
The Consumer Revolution

Empire transformed everyday life in Britain between 1688 and c.1730. Goods that had been royal luxuries in the early seventeenth century — tea, coffee, sugar, tobacco, chocolate — became widely available and affordable to the middle classes by the early eighteenth century. This was a consumer revolution. It was made possible by the expansion of colonial trade, the growth of the merchant navy, and the increasing use of enslaved African labour on Caribbean and American plantations that kept prices low.

Sugar consumption in England grew dramatically. By the early eighteenth century, England consumed more sugar per head than any other European country. Sugar sweetened tea, preserved jams, and featured in cooking in ways previously impossible. This demand drove the expansion of Caribbean sugar plantations, which in turn required more enslaved labour. The consumer revolution in Britain and the expansion of the slave trade were not separate phenomena: they were structurally connected.

Coffee Houses and Political Debate

Coffee houses were one of the most important social institutions of early eighteenth-century Britain. By 1700, London had over 2,000 coffee houses. They served as meeting points for merchants, politicians, writers and intellectuals. Business was conducted, newspapers were read aloud, and political opinions were formed. Lloyd’s coffee house (founded by Edward Lloyd) became the centre of marine insurance, eventually evolving into Lloyd’s of London — demonstrating how imperial trade and coffee-house culture were inseparable.

Key Fact

By 1700, London had over 2,000 coffee houses. They were centres of political debate, commerce (Lloyd’s marine insurance), and press culture (newspapers read aloud). Coffee itself was an imperial product from the Middle East and later the Caribbean; the houses exemplified how empire shaped domestic British culture.

Slave Ports and Popular Involvement in the Trade

The slave trade was not confined to a small merchant elite. Bristol, Liverpool and London developed as slave ports: cities whose civic wealth, employment, and supply chains were deeply entangled with slave-trading voyages. Shipbuilders, rope-makers, ironmongers, textile merchants, insurance brokers, and dock workers all participated indirectly in the trade. By the early eighteenth century Bristol had temporarily overtaken London as the leading slaving port. Ordinary British people invested in voyages, bought enslaved persons’ labour-produced goods, and worked in industries that supported the trade.

The slave trade required ideological justification. From the late seventeenth century, ideas of racial hierarchy — classifying people by skin colour and assigning them different capacities and rights — became more systematised in British thought. These ideas affected settled Black communities in Britain. A small but visible Black population lived in London and other cities, often as domestic servants, sailors or musicians. Some had been brought to Britain from the colonies. They faced discrimination, legal insecurity (their status in English law was ambiguous until the Somerset Case of 1772), and the pervasive assumption of inferiority promoted by pro-slavery ideology.

Key Fact

The consumer revolution and the slave trade were structurally linked: cheap sugar required enslaved labour on Caribbean plantations; British demand for sugar, tobacco and cotton drove demand for enslaved Africans. Critics including early Quaker abolitionists recognised this connection explicitly.

Opposition to slavery in this period was limited but not absent. Quakers (the Society of Friends) were the earliest organised opponents: their 1727–1731 meetings began formally condemning the slave trade. Individual writers such as Mary Astell commented critically on the contradictions of a society that celebrated liberty while enslaving others. Resistance also came from enslaved people themselves: rebellions on plantations were recorded throughout the Caribbean, and some enslaved people in Britain sought freedom through the courts. The abolitionist movement would not gain mass political momentum until the 1780s, but its intellectual roots lie in this period.

Press Culture and Political Activism

Coffee houses were inseparable from the growth of print culture. London’s first daily newspaper, the Daily Courant, appeared in 1702. By the 1710s and 1720s, journals like The Spectator (edited by Joseph Addison and Richard Steele) reached a wide readership through coffee houses, where copies were passed from reader to reader. Jonathan Swift’s political satires circulated in the same networks. This press culture created a new public sphere in which political opinions could be formed and challenged outside Parliament. The coffee house was the physical space where print culture and oral debate combined.

The same coffee-house networks that debated politics and insurance also debated the slave trade. The contradictions were not invisible to contemporaries. Olaudah Equiano — born in what is now Nigeria, enslaved as a child, eventually able to purchase his freedom — lived for periods in London and later became one of the most important voices against the slave trade. His autobiography (1789) was published too late for this period, but Equiano’s earlier life overlapped with the world of the coffee houses and shows that the enslaved diaspora had a presence and a voice in British cities even when their legal status was deeply insecure.
exam_tip_html: For questions about the social and political impact of empire, link the consumer revolution, the slave ports and the development of racial ideology as connected consequences of the same imperial trade system. Examiners at the highest level expect you to show contradictions — Britain celebrated itself as a land of liberty (the Bill of Rights, parliamentary government) while participating massively in the trade in enslaved Africans. Connecting these contradictions is exactly what the highest-band answers do.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Empire transformed British daily life: tea, coffee, sugar, tobacco and chocolate moved from aristocratic luxuries to middle-class staples, creating a consumer revolution that was structurally dependent on enslaved African labour on colonial plantations.
  • Coffee houses (over 2,000 in London by 1700) became centres of political debate, press culture and commerce, including Lloyd’s marine insurance — demonstrating how imperial trade shaped domestic British institutions.
  • The slave trade was embedded across British society through slave ports (Bristol, Liverpool, London), supply industries and investment; early opposition came from Quaker meetings (1727–1731) and individual writers, while enslaved people resisted on plantations and in courts.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of coffee houses in early eighteenth-century Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. Lloyd's coffee house became the centre of marine insurance, showing how commerce and coffee-house culture were inseparable). Secure: Correct feature with some supporting information. Developing: Vague reference without specific detail. Emerging: Incorrect or irrelevant response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the consumer revolution in Britain in the period 1688–c.1730.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. sugar consumption made England the highest per-head consumer in Europe; tea moved from aristocratic luxury to middle-class staple) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

practice_questions.text: Explain why ordinary British people were more widely involved in the slave trade than is sometimes assumed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation covering slave ports, supply industries, investment, consumer demand for slave-produced goods, with precise evidence (Bristol, Liverpool statistics, Lloyd's). Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence; at least one dimension explained. Developing: Some explanation with basic evidence; may be descriptive. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: How significant was the consumer revolution for changing British society in the period 1688–c.1730? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument evaluating the consumer revolution's domestic social impact (diet, coffee houses, press culture) alongside its dependency on imperial trade and enslaved labour, with judgement on the limits of 'revolution' and counter-arguments. Secure: Clear argument with evidence across more than one dimension. Developing: Some argument; may focus on only one aspect. Emerging: Simple points with limited evidence.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why racial hierarchy ideas developed in Britain during this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation showing the ideological function of racial hierarchy in justifying the slave trade, its impact on settled Black communities in Britain, and the legal ambiguity of their status. Secure: Clear explanation with relevant evidence. Developing: Basic reason with limited evidence. Emerging: Vague or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of early opposition to the slave trade in this period.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. Quaker meetings formally condemned the slave trade from 1727–1731; enslaved people themselves resisted through plantation rebellions and legal challenges) each with accurate detail. Secure: Two features, at least one with detail. Developing: One feature with detail, or two without. Emerging: Vague or inaccurate response.

knowledge_checks.q: Approximately how many coffee houses did London have by 1700?
Which religious group were the earliest organised opponents of the slave trade in Britain?
Lloyd's coffee house, founded by Edward Lloyd, became the centre of _____ insurance in London.
By the early eighteenth century, Britain's consumption of _____ per head was higher than any other European country.
Match each term to its description:
right: Cities like Bristol and Liverpool whose wealth was entangled with the slave trade
Social venues for political debate, news and commerce
Wider access to imperial goods for the middle classes

flashcard_questions.a: The spread of imperial goods (tea, sugar, coffee, tobacco) to the British middle classes from the late 17th century

flashcard_questions.q: How many coffee houses did London have by 1700?
What did Lloyd's coffee house become?
flashcard_questions.a: The centre of marine insurance, later evolving into Lloyd's of London

flashcard_questions.q: Which city temporarily overtook London as the leading British slaving port in the early 18th century?
How was British sugar consumption structurally linked to the slave trade?
flashcard_questions.a: Caribbean sugar required enslaved African labour; British demand drove demand for enslaved people

flashcard_questions.q: When did Quaker meetings begin formally condemning the slave trade?
What was the legal status of Black people in Britain in this period?
flashcard_questions.a: Ambiguous — not resolved until the Somerset Case (1772)

flashcard_questions.q: Name one writer who criticised the contradiction between British liberty and slavery in this period.
Why did the consumer revolution require enslaved labour?
flashcard_questions.a: Cheap colonial goods (sugar, tobacco) depended on the unpaid labour of enslaved Africans on plantations

flashcard_questions.q: How did enslaved people themselves resist in this period?
flashcard_questions.a: Through plantation rebellions in the Caribbean and legal challenges in British courts

glossary_terms.definition: The change in British society from the late seventeenth century in which a wider range of imported goods became available and consumption of exotic produce became a marker of social status.
Establishments selling coffee and other hot drinks, which became centres of political debate, commerce and news-sharing in London and other British cities from the 1660s.
British port cities (particularly Bristol, Liverpool and London) whose economic prosperity was significantly built on profits from the trade in enslaved Africans and colonial goods.
A formerly enslaved African who became a celebrated writer and abolitionist; his autobiography (1789) described the slave trade and his life in detail.
